title: The child on the leaf
hookLine: a sage is breathed in and out by a child on a banyan leaf; why Hindus see time as cycles that rest in God
carry: time breathes in cycles, and rests in god
tomorrow: why is half of Shiva a woman?
last: ARJUNA'S WIND: THE MIND FOLLOWS THE BREATH.

lines: A BABY ON A BANYAN LEAF.
cards: The world has ended. Not in fire: in water. A sage named Markandeya is swimming alone in a dark ocean with no shore, for what feels like ages.
Then, on the water, a banyan tree, and on one of its leaves, a baby. Glowing, calm, sucking his own toe. Markandeya swims closer.
The baby breathes in, and the sage is pulled into his body like a mosquito on the wind.

teach.b: Inside the child, Markandeya finds everything. Mountains, rivers, cities, even his own little hermitage. The whole world, alive inside one small body.
Then the baby breathes out, and the sage tumbles back into the dark water, and there's the child again on the leaf, smiling. This is from the Bhagavata Purana, and the child is Vishnu.

Here's the teaching under it, one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: time moves in cycles. The world isn't made once and finished. It comes out, lives, dissolves, and rests in God, and then comes out again, age after age.

teach.h: BETWEEN WORLDS, IT RESTS IN GOD.
teach.b: Between worlds, it's often pictured as Vishnu resting on the great ocean. Nothing is lost there; everything is held, waiting for the next breath. Now the word.

Kumbhaka, from kumbha, a clay water jar: the breath resting still, like water in a jar. Every breath has two small pauses, one at the top after the in-breath, and one at the bottom after the out-breath.
Some teachers like to read them as tiny echoes of that great rest.

teach.h: TWO SOFT COUNTS, NEVER A STRAIN.
teach.b: Keep it gentle: two soft counts, no clamping the throat. The old yoga texts describe long holds, but those were taught one to one, by a teacher watching closely. If a pause makes you anxious or short of air, skip it.

teach.h: TIME BREATHES IN CYCLES, AND RESTS IN GOD.
teach.b: If you're pregnant, or have high blood pressure, or a heart or lung condition, leave the holds out and just notice where the pauses would be. For Hindus, a stop isn't the end of the story.
It's the world resting in God before the next breath.

how: Hindu teaching pictures time in great cycles of creation and dissolution, with the world resting in God between them; images of the child on the banyan leaf recall Markandeya's vision. In yoga, kumbhaka, gentle breath retention, is taught gradually by a teacher.

o: a soft pause in the breath, like water resting in a jar
a song sung at the end of the day
a slow count for the in-breath

games.q: match the story to the teaching.
p: the sage alone in the flood
Vishnu, holding the whole world inside
the dissolving, when the world rests in God

s: in Hindu teaching, the world was made once and will end for good
time moves in cycles: the world comes out, dissolves, rests in God, and comes out again.
inside the child, Markandeya found the whole world, even his own hermitage
sky, mountains, rivers and his little hut, all inside one small body.
a beginner should hold the breath as long as possible
two soft counts, never a strain. long holds were taught one to one by a teacher.

games.q: a friend hears that Hindus believe the world ends and begins again, and says that sounds bleak. what fits today's teaching?
o: it isn't bleak: between worlds, everything rests in God, like the world Markandeya found held inside the child.
it means the world ends forever, so nothing really matters.
it's only a poem about seasons; Hindus don't really teach cycles of time.
games.why: in Hindu teaching, dissolution isn't loss. the world rests in God, then is breathed out again.

practice: Breathe in for four and rest at the top for two, then breathe out for six and rest at the bottom for two, and let the next breath come.
If the holds feel easy, keep them; if not, just notice where the top and bottom are without stopping, and either way is the practice. Look for the still point, like the child resting on the leaf.

wordCard.voice: Kumbhaka. From kumbha, a water jar. The pause in the breath, where everything rests for a moment.
